sol_lobbying.title: Statutes of limitation for child sexual abuse, and the lobbying against reform
summary_facts: The US Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million lobbying in eight northeastern states from 2011 to 2018, including against limitation-period reform: Pennsylvania $5,322,979; New York $2,912,772; Connecticut $875,261; New Jersey $633,458; Massachusetts $537,551; New Hampshire $134,345; Maine $124,260; Rhode Island $61,961 (report 'Church Influencing State', commissioned by four law firms representing survivors, from public lobbying filings, reported by NBC News June 2019).

In Pennsylvania the Catholic Conference spent over $7.6 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024 and the Insurance Federation of Pennsylvania nearly $20.7 million (both lobby on other issues too); as of February 2025 Pennsylvania still had no revival window, after a 2021 constitutional amendment failed because the state did not advertise it (Spotlight PA).

The Boy Scouts of America's national organization spent about $2.5 million on lobbying from 2011 to 2017, and the Scouts and a local council spent $486,505 lobbying in Pennsylvania from 2016 to 2018 (USA TODAY / Arizona Republic / Center for Public Integrity, 2019).

In 2017 the American Insurance Association spent $130,000 lobbying New York on issues including the Child Victims Act; AIA, Liberty Mutual and Zurich together spent more than $375,000 lobbying Albany that year (NBC New York I-Team, 29 March 2018).

Child USA counts 33 US jurisdictions (30 states, DC and two territories) that have passed revival windows or revival laws for child sexual abuse claims since 2002; Colorado's, Kentucky's and Utah's were later held unconstitutional.
New York's one-year window (opened 14 August 2019, extended twice to 14 August 2021) produced more than 9,000 lawsuits (AP, August 2021).

Maryland removed its limitation period for child sexual abuse claims in 2023; after more than 3,100 suits, the legislature in 2025 cut damage caps from $1.5m to $700,000 for private institutions and from $890,000 to $400,000 for public ones, effective 1 June 2025 (Maryland Matters).

All Australian states and territories removed limitation periods for child sexual abuse civil claims between 2015 (Victoria) and 2018 (Western Australia, South Australia, Queensland), following the Royal Commission's 2015 Redress and Civil Litigation report.

England and Wales removed the three-year limitation period for child sexual abuse personal-injury claims through section 96 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026, in force 29 June 2026; Scotland had done so in 2017.

bankruptcy_shield.title: Bankruptcy and asset transfers as a shield against abuse claims
summary_facts: This dataset lists 39 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders that filed for Chapter 11 between the Archdiocese of Portland's first filing (6 July 2004) and Fresno (July 2025), plus San Diego's second filing (2024); Rochester's 2019 filing was the 20th diocese, so more than half came after the 2019 wave of revival windows.

Filings often came just before a trial or deposition: Portland (hours before two trials, 2004), San Diego (hours before the first of ~150 suits, 2007), Wilmington (the day before trial, 2009), Milwaukee (two days before the archbishop's deposition, 2011), Baltimore (two days before Maryland's Child Victims Act took effect, 2023).

Boy Scouts of America: filed 18 February 2020; more than 82,000 abuse claims; $2.46 billion plan confirmed 8 September 2022 with third-party releases for local councils, insurers and churches; Third Circuit upheld May 2025; US Supreme Court denied review 12 January 2026.

In Harrington v. Purdue Pharma (27 June 2024), the US Supreme Court held the Bankruptcy Code does not authorise releases of claims against non-debtor third parties without the claimants' consent. About 144 BSA survivors had argued the Scouts plan used a similar mechanism to shield local councils and churches; the BSA plan was nonetheless upheld by the Third Circuit (May 2025) and the Supreme Court declined review (12 January 2026).

In 2007 Archbishop Timothy Dolan asked the Vatican to move $57 million into a Milwaukee cemetery trust for 'improved protection of these funds from any legal claim and liability'; the Vatican approved it five weeks later (documents released in bankruptcy, July 2013).
Archdiocese of Santa Fe transferred assets worth over $150 million into trusts and incorporated parishes before filing; in October 2020 the judge let survivors pursue fraudulent-transfer claims.

inquiry_waves.title: Inquiry waves — when each country first investigated institutional child sexual abuse
summary_facts: The first official national-level inquiries into institutional child sexual abuse came in Canada (Hughes Royal Commission, provincial, 1989) and Ireland (Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse, 1999-2009); most of Europe followed only after the 2010 wave (Germany, Belgium, Netherlands, Austria).

Many 'national' Catholic inquiries were commissioned by the Church itself rather than the state: John Jay (US, 2004), Deetman (Netherlands, 2011), MHG (Germany, 2018), CIASE (France, 2021), Strecht (Portugal, 2023), University of Zurich (Switzerland, 2023). Spain's 2023 Ombudsman report is a rare state inquiry.

Where inquiries used population surveys, estimates were far higher than church records: France 216,000 minors abused by clergy (330,000 incl. lay staff) versus 3,000 identified in 2020; Spain 0.6% of adults abused by a priest or religious (survey of 8,013); Netherlands 10,000-20,000.
New Zealand's Royal Commission (final report 24 July 2024) estimated 113,000-253,000 people abused in state and faith-based care 1950-1999.
Italy has no official national statistics or inquiry; the Italian Bishops' Conference said in 2012 its priests had no obligation to report to police under the Lateran concordat.
Poland's State Commission (2019 law) reported in August 2022 that church files sent to the Vatican were beyond its reach and canon law destroys files ten years after conviction.

tourism_displacement.title: Tourism displacement — how child sex tourism moved as enforcement rose
summary_facts: Svay Pak, Cambodia: child prostitution there grew in the early 2000s 'after child prostitution in Thailand was cracked down upon'; the 22 January 2003 raid was advertised in advance and nearly all children were moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville; by 2011 the trade had gone underground (Wikipedia, citing Telegraph, AHRC, Dateline NBC, CNN).

Offender-country laws came in a wave in the 1990s-2000s: Germany 1993, Australia 1994, Canada 1997, Japan 1999, US PROTECT Act 2003, UK Sexual Offences Act 2003, NZ 2005, Ireland 2017; ECPAT counted 44 countries with extraterritorial laws in 2008.

In the Philippines IJM found establishment-based child sex trafficking fell 79-86% in target cities 2006-2016, while monthly Philippine IP addresses used for child sexual exploitation rose more than 12-fold from 2014 to 2017 (IJM, May 2020).
Europol (June 2020): travel restrictions 'likely prevented offenders from travelling and so have shifted their focus' online; IOCTA 2020: 'livestreaming is becoming mainstream'.

Displacement within countries is also documented: Manila's 1992 Ermita closure pushed businesses to Angeles City; Gambian traffickers moved child sex tourists into private residences outside tourist zones; Madagascar saw increases after Mozambique tightened laws.

protected_status.title: Protected status — delay between first report and first official action
summary_facts: Across the 42 cases here with both years documented (median 12.5 years), the gap between the first documented report to police, church, employer or officials and the first official action ranges from months (Dutroux 1995→1996) to over five decades (Cyril Smith 1968→2012, Savile 1958→2012).

Repeated mechanisms: a lenient deal (Epstein's 2007 non-prosecution agreement), police closing an inquiry on orders from above (Mount Cashel 1975), officials passing over a complaint because the accused was 'a very important, powerful man' (Cyril Smith 1968), church superiors moving the accused (Ridsdale, O'Grady, Hullermann, Smyth), media silence (Savile, Kitagawa), cross-border flight (Leifer, Nithyananda), and intimidation or killing of witnesses (Asaram, Omotoso).
In several cases action came only after the accused died: Savile (died 2011, Yewtree 2012), Cyril Smith (died 2010, CPS 2012), Kitagawa (died 2019, probe 2023).

intergovernmental_shielding.title: Intergovernmental shielding — states protecting nationals or officials from prosecution
summary_facts: UN peacekeepers fall under their own country's criminal jurisdiction; the UN can only repatriate and bar them. In Haiti at least 134 Sri Lankan soldiers were accused of abusing nine children (2004-2007) and none were convicted; in the Central African Republic 41 Burundian and Gabonese troops identified over abuse of at least 98 girls were sent home uncharged.

In 2025 the UN recorded 26 allegations against military contingents involving 9 child victims; for most, the troop-contributing country's action was still 'pending' (Secretary-General report A/80/644).

Holy See diplomats accused of child-abuse offences were recalled and dealt with in Vatican City rather than local courts: Wesołowski (Dominican Republic, 2013; Vatican refused extradition to Poland), Capella (Washington, 2017; immune in the US, convicted by Vatican tribunal 2018). The Holy See waived immunity once, for Ventura in France (2019).
South Korea's Seoul High Court refused US extradition of Welcome to Video operator Son Jong-woo on 6 July 2020 after he had served 18 months.
Morocco's king pardoned Spanish child rapist Daniel Galván in 2013 as a diplomatic gesture to Spain; he left on an expired passport; Spain later refused to extradite him.
